## Hourly Income of Owners and Employees {#sec-appendix-gap}

```{r}
#| label: gap-data
#| include: false

# Run this chunk before tbl-gap-industry.
# Rebuilds the industry-year gap data from panel_final (waves 1 to 21).
gap_cells <- panel_final |>
  dplyr::filter(as.integer(as.character(wave)) <= 21) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    year_num = as.integer(as.character(year)),
    industry = stringr::str_to_sentence(as.character(industry_19categories_jbmi61)),
    hourly_income = dplyr::if_else(
      hours_weekly_all_job_jbhruc > 0,
      income_labour_and_business / (52 * hours_weekly_all_job_jbhruc),
      NA_real_
    ),
    is_small_employee = is_employee %in% 1 & small_single_site %in% 1,
    is_small_owner = owner_with_employees %in% 1 & dplyr::coalesce(small_wp == 1, FALSE) & !is.na(hourly_income)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(industry))

gap_kt <- gap_cells |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    wage_employee = median(hrwge_main_clean[is_small_employee], na.rm = TRUE),
    income_owner = median(hourly_income[is_small_owner], na.rm = TRUE),
    n_owner = sum(is_small_owner),
    share_migrant = mean(migrant[is_small_owner] %in% 1),
    .by = c(industry, year_num)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(n_owner >= 10, wage_employee > 0, income_owner > 0) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gap_hourly = log(wage_employee) - log(income_owner))

gap_by_industry <- gap_kt |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_years = dplyr::n(),
    gap = stats::weighted.mean(gap_hourly, n_owner),
    se = sqrt(sum(n_owner^2 * (gap_hourly - gap)^2)) / sum(n_owner),
    share_migrant = stats::weighted.mean(share_migrant, n_owner),
    .by = industry
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(n_years >= 3)

time_industries <- gap_kt |>
  dplyr::count(industry) |>
  dplyr::filter(n >= 10) |>
  dplyr::pull(industry)

# Checks against the numbers quoted in the text
nrow(gap_kt)                                          # 273 industry-years
stats::weighted.mean(gap_kt$gap_hourly, gap_kt$n_owner)  # about -0.085
mean(gap_kt$gap_hourly > 0)                           # about 0.37

# The two industries with the largest migrant share of owners, quoted in the text
gap_top <- dplyr::slice_max(gap_by_industry, share_migrant, n = 2)
```

The regressions in @tbl-b2-main compare owners with employees in general, conditional on the controls. As a complementary descriptive measure, we compare the income of employees in small independent workplaces with that of owners with employees in the same industry and year.

$$
\text{WorkerOwnerGap}_{kt} = \underset{kt}{\text{Median}}\left(\log w^{\,\text{Employee, SmallSingleSite}}\right) - \underset{kt}{\text{Median}}\left(\log y^{\,\text{OwnerWithEmployees}}\right)
$$ {#eq-worker-owner-gap}

where the medians are taken over employees and owners within industry $k$ and year $t$. Both terms are measured per hour of work. $w$ is the employee's hourly wage in their main job, and $y$ is the owner's annual labour and business income divided by their annual hours, since owners typically work longer hours than employees. Medians are used so that the measure remains defined when some owners report business losses.[^gapcells] A positive gap indicates that employees earn more per hour than owners in the same industry.

[^gapcells]: The gap is computed only for industry-years with at least 10 owners with employees, to avoid imprecise estimates from small cells.

@tbl-gap-industry shows that the gap varies considerably across industries. Employees earn more per hour than owners in low-margin industries dominated by small businesses, including accommodation and food services, agriculture, retail trade and other services. In accommodation and food services, employees earn around 30 per cent more per hour than the owners of small businesses in the same industry. In professional industries such as health care, finance and professional services, owners earn substantially more per hour than employees. The ordering does not follow the share of migrant owners. The two industries with the largest migrant shares of owners are `r tolower(gap_top$industry[1])` (`r fmt_num(100 * gap_top$share_migrant[1], 0)` per cent) and `r tolower(gap_top$industry[2])` (`r fmt_num(100 * gap_top$share_migrant[2], 0)` per cent), with gaps of `r fmt_num(gap_top$gap[1], 2)` and `r fmt_num(gap_top$gap[2], 2)` log points.

Across all 273 industry-years, owners with employees earn more than employees of small independent workplaces, by about 9 per cent per hour (a weighted mean gap of $-0.085$ log points) and about 60 per cent per year ($-0.472$ log points). The much larger annual difference reflects the longer hours worked by owners. Employees nonetheless earn more per hour than owners in 37 per cent of industry-years, concentrated in the low-margin industries at the top of @tbl-gap-industry.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gap-industry
#| tbl-cap: "Median hourly income gap between employees and owners with employees, by industry."
#| echo: false

fmt3 <- \(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)

gap_by_year <- gap_kt |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_years = dplyr::n(),
    share_positive = mean(gap_hourly > 0),
    .by = industry
  )

gap_industries <- gap_by_industry |>
  dplyr::select(industry, gap, se, share_migrant) |>
  dplyr::left_join(gap_by_year, by = "industry") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(gap))

gap_overall <- tibble::tibble(
  industry = "All industry-years",
  gap = stats::weighted.mean(gap_kt$gap_hourly, gap_kt$n_owner),
  se = NA_real_,
  share_migrant = stats::weighted.mean(gap_kt$share_migrant, gap_kt$n_owner),
  n_years = nrow(gap_kt),
  share_positive = mean(gap_kt$gap_hourly > 0)
)

# One row per industry, with the standard error of its mean gap on the row
# below; the pooled row has no standard error
gap_row <- \(d) tibble::tibble(
  Industry = c(d$industry, if (!is.na(d$se)) ""),
  `Industry-years` = c(as.character(d$n_years), if (!is.na(d$se)) ""),
  `Mean gap (log points)` = c(fmt3(d$gap), if (!is.na(d$se)) paste0("(", fmt3(d$se), ")")),
  `Years with positive gap` = c(scales::percent(d$share_positive, accuracy = 1), if (!is.na(d$se)) ""),
  `Migrant share of owners` = c(scales::percent(d$share_migrant, accuracy = 1), if (!is.na(d$se)) "")
)
gap_display <- dplyr::bind_rows(gap_industries, gap_overall) |>
  split(seq_len(nrow(gap_industries) + 1)) |>
  purrr::map_dfr(gap_row)

tinytable::tt(gap_display) |>
  tinytable::theme_empty() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(i = 0, line = "tb") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(i = 2 * nrow(gap_industries), line = "b") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(i = nrow(gap_display), line = "b") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 1, align = "l") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "c") |>
  pair_se_rows()
```

::: {.notes}
*Notes:* This table reports the median hourly income gap of @eq-worker-owner-gap by industry, in HILDA waves 1 to 21. The gap is the median log hourly wage of employees in small single-site workplaces minus the median log hourly income of owners with employees in small workplaces, within each industry and year; a positive gap means that employees earn more per hour than owners. The mean gap for each industry is the average over its industry-years with at least 10 owners, weighted by the number of owners, and industries with fewer than three such years are not listed. The standard error in parentheses treats industry-years as independent and is therefore indicative. The last row pools all industry-years.
:::

## Assimilation Decay Horizons: Supporting Literature {#sec-appendix-assimilation}

@sec-loo-shares searches over the decay parameter $\lambda$ in the range $[0, 0.30]$ for a single pooled rate and $[0, 0.50]$ for origin-specific rates. This range is informed by a broader literature on the horizon over which migrants' earnings, occupational status and linguistic proficiency converge toward native-born benchmarks.

@chiswick_effect_1978 and @schuetze_immigration_2007 established that immigrant earnings typically converge to native benchmarks within 10 to 15 years, consistent with @akee_immigrant_2026, who find, using administrative panel data in the United States, that recent cohorts achieve parity within 10 years, though earlier cohorts exhibit strong growth without complete convergence. Examining job search mechanics, @bowlus_immigrant_2016 estimates that immigrants take an average of 13 years to match native job offer arrival rates. Longer horizons are also evident. @arellano-bover_role_2026 show that the overall wage gap closes only after 27 to 29 years, with convergence and long-term prosperity driven primarily by firm-to-firm mobility and climbing the employer ladder. In the Australian context, @chiswick_longitudinal_2005 document a U-shaped occupational trajectory, where an initial drop in status due to imperfect skill transferability is followed by gradual earnings recovery. @schuetze_immigration_2007 found that self-employment rates for specific immigrant cohorts steadily increase with their time spent in the host country (main countries of the study include the United States, Canada and Australia), typically catching up to native-born rates within 10 to 20 years of arrival. Although self-employed immigrants tend to outperform their native counterparts, @schuetze_immigration_2007 attributes this to the fact that the countries used their analysis, as well as many other developed nations, use special visas and entrepreneurial entry requirements as tools to attract foreign talent, but notes that broader market structures and local economic conditions remain the strongest overall drivers of success. @breunig_immigrant_2013 examines the wage gap on entry and wage assimilation of immigrants to Australia by comparing results from standard cross-sectional models (Heckman selection model) with panel data estimators (Fixed Effects, Random Effects and Hausman-Taylor (HT) estimator) to account for unobserved individual heterogeneity. They found that there is a wage gap for immigrant men from English-speaking backgrounds, in contrast with previous research which has found no wage gap and wage assimilation occurs slowly for all immigrant groups, but is much faster for MES men than for MNES group.

Evidence on identity and linguistic assimilation provides further guidance on empirical decay horizons. @abramitzky_immigrants_2020 show that naming convergence between immigrant and native parents occurs over roughly 20 years. Language acquisition follows a similar pattern. @kulkarni_english_2014 find that English proficiency rises from 45 to 55% at arrival to 60 to 63% after 5 years, and reaches 66 to 67% after 10 years, reflecting rapid initial gains followed by slow gains thereafter [@espinosa_determinants_1997; @kossoudji_english_1988; @stevens_age_1999; @guven_age_2015]. Wage convergence, however, proceeds more slowly for non-English-speaking migrants once individual heterogeneity is controlled for, with older arrival cohorts experiencing persistent structural gaps [@breunig_immigrant_2013].

Furthermore, @chiswick_longitudinal_2005 suggests that immigrants moving between similar institutional contexts, such as an English-speaking Canadian entering the United States, face minimal initial downward mobility. For these main English-speaking migrants, divergence from native-born workers depends primarily on arrival timing, not skill acquisition. Indeed, the literature on Australia and the United States documents "negative" assimilation among immigrants from English-speaking developed countries, where initial wage premiums decay over time [@chiswick_negative_2011; @chiswick_negative_2011-1]. In Australia, migrants from English-speaking developed countries experience a relative earnings decline over their duration of residence, with earnings 5.5% lower for the 1988 cohort than the 1998 cohort over ten years [@chiswick_negative_2011].

Broader socio-cultural integration reflects a similar pattern. While shared values facilitate smoother initial settlement [@nakhaie_language_2020], full identity assimilation can remain non-converged even after decades abroad [@scott_transnational_2004]. Anglophone immigrants in Australia, and UK-born immigrants specifically, nonetheless exhibit employment outcomes and qualification returns nearly identical to those of native-born Australians [@colic-peisker_ethnics_2011]. Identity and cultural assimilation operate on much longer horizons than economic, occupational and linguistic assimilation, so our empirical focus in the main text centres strictly on the latter.

@tbl-lambda-calibration reports the five best-fitting values of $\lambda$ within each of the three decay specifications described in @sec-loo-shares, alongside the mean squared error achieved via cross-validation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lambda-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Best-fitting $\\lambda$ estimates for three specifications."
#| echo: false

mse_ref <- cal$type1 |> filter(lambda == 0) |> pull(mse)

# Half-life in years; a zero decay rate never halves, shown as infinity
half_life <- \(l) ifelse(l == 0, "∞", sprintf("%.1f", log(2) / l))

t1 <- cal$type1 |>
  arrange(mse) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    spec = "Type 1",
    lam = sprintf("%.2f", lambda),
    lam_mes = "",
    lam_mn = "",
    hl = half_life(lambda),
    hl_mes = "",
    hl_mn = "",
    mse = mse
  )

t2 <- cal$type2 |>
  arrange(mse) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    spec = "Type 2",
    lam = "",
    lam_mes = sprintf("%.2f", lambda_mes),
    lam_mn = sprintf("%.2f", lambda_mnes),
    hl = "",
    hl_mes = half_life(lambda_mes),
    hl_mn = half_life(lambda_mnes),
    mse = mse
  )

ref <- tibble(
  spec = "Type 0",
  lam = "0.00",
  lam_mes = "",
  lam_mn = "",
  hl = "--",
  hl_mes = "",
  hl_mn = "",
  mse = mse_ref
)

tab <- bind_rows(ref, t1, t2) |>
  mutate(
    mse_fmt = sprintf("%.8f", mse),
    delta = sprintf("%+.2f", 1e5 * (mse - mse_ref)),
    spec = if_else(duplicated(spec), "", spec)
  )

tab |>
  select(spec, lam, hl, lam_mes, lam_mn, hl_mes, hl_mn, mse_fmt, delta) |>
  setNames(
    c(
      "Type",
      "$lambda$",
      "Half-life",
      "$lambda_\"MES\"$",
      "$lambda_\"MNES\"$",
      "Half-life (MES)",
      "Half-life (MNES)",
      "MSE",
      "Difference (in $10^5$ scale)"
    )
  ) |>
  tt(
    width = c(0.10, 0.09, 0.09, 0.09, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10, 0.16, 0.17)
  ) |>
  style_tt(i = c(2, 7), j = 2:9, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = 0, line = "tb") |>
  style_tt(i = c(2, 7), line = "t") |>
  style_tt(j = 2:9, align = "r") |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = FALSE, align = "c") |>
  style_tt(i = 0, line = "b")
```

::: {.notes}
*Notes:* This table reports the five best-fitting decay rates for each specification of @sec-loo-shares, ranked by the five-fold cross-validated mean squared error (MSE) of log hourly wages. Type 0 applies no decay ($\lambda = 0$), Type 1 a single pooled rate to all migrant owners and Type 2 separate rates to MES and MNES owners. Half-lives are $\ln 2 / \lambda$ in years. *Difference* is the change in MSE from the Type 0 benchmark, multiplied by $10^5$. The selected values are in bold.
:::

The Type 2 specification, which allows the decay rate to vary by English-speaking background, achieves the lowest mean squared error of the three, but its gain over no decay is small relative to the error itself. We therefore use the plain owner shares (Type 0) for the main employee wage estimates and report Types 1 and 2 as robustness checks.
